extracted.subtask_description: Extract and summarize substantive epistemological principles argued in a philosophical essay about the relativity of knowledge, consciousness, and the limits of conceivability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness requires limitation/difference
rubrics_metrics.description: All thought is limitation; whatever we conceive is, by the very act of conception, regarded as finite. To speak of a Conception of the Infinite is at once to affirm those conditions (limits) and to deny them, producing a self-contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation and examples: since no finite part can be a constituent of an infinite whole, conceiving the Infinite as a positive object of thought entails contradictions. The supposed 'infinite' would have to be both limited (to be an object of consciousness) and unlimited (to be infinite), which is impossible. Thus conceivability requires distinguishing features/limits; anything lacking them cannot be conceived as a positive object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness is essentially relational (subject–object)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consciousness is possible only in the form of a relation: there must be a Subject (person conscious) and an Object (thing of which he is conscious). Each exists only insofar as it is related to the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: one cannot be conscious of the Absolute as such, because to know identity between an object given in relation to consciousness and one existing independently would require comparing two objects, one of which would be outside consciousness — a contradiction. Thus any purported positive consciousness of the Absolute is self-contradictory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognition requires distinction, relation, and likeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Every complete act of consciousness implies three conditions: distinction (difference), relation, and likeness (recognition/assimilation). A mental state must be known as distinct from others, related (e.g., by succession), and recognized as like certain previous states to become an idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequences/examples: classification and assimilation are essential to intelligence; without likeness (recognition) cognition would be chaotic. Cognition emerges gradually (infant examples): novel objects are known insofar as they can be assimilated to prior categories; degrees of completeness of classification determine degree of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Unconditioned/Absolute is unthinkable by the conditions of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Because thought requires distinction, relation, and likeness (conditions that constitute consciousness), the Unconditioned (Absolute, Infinite) presents none of these and is therefore 'trebly unthinkable' — unthinkable by difference, relation, and likeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is argued formally: the Absolute cannot be classed with conditioned things; to think of it as a kind would make it conditioned and thus not absolute; to suppose plurality of Absolutes produces contradiction. Therefore the Unconditioned cannot be known as an object of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life and intelligence as continuous adjustment of internal to external relations (basis for relativity of knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Life, in abstract, is definable as the continuous adjustment of internal relations to external relations; intelligence is the establishment of more varied and complete adjustments between internal (subjective) and external (objective) relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: physiological homeostasis, sensory-guided predation, tool manufacture, chemistry, and scientific theory all instantiate internal responses coordinated to external co-existences and sequences. Since cognition consists of forming relations in consciousness parallel to external relations, knowledge is necessarily relative (limited to relations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth is correspondence of subjective to objective relations; error is absence of such correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: What we call truth, guiding successful action, is simply the accurate correspondence of subjective relations to objective relations; error is the absence of such accurate correspondence, leading to failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and examples: organisms act successfully when internal states reliably track external regularities (e.g., scent→nutriment), and scientific explanations are successful when mental relations coordinate with external relations (gunpowder explosion, projectile theory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of knowledge presupposes the object denied (argument presupposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that show the Absolute is unknowable nonetheless presuppose a positive consciousness of something beyond the relative: to deny knowledge of the Absolute presumes the concept of an Absolute (the Noumenon) as the correlate of the Phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique: if the Unconditioned is used throughout as the antithesis of the Relative in arguments, then those arguments already assume a positive (though perhaps indefinite) conception of the Unconditioned; an argument concluding that the term has no meaning would be self-destructive because it relies on that very meaning in its construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative correlatives are not mere negations but contain residual positive consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a correlative is formulated negatively (e.g., the Infinite, the Inconceivable), the mind retains a consciousness of 'some kind of being' — the negative removes limits but does not abolish the awareness of something that is limited's complement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: the notion of the Unlimited abolishes consciousness of limits but not the consciousness of some kind of being; hence negative correlatives (the inconceivable, the Absolute) are not mere nonentities or pure abstractions but have a positive residue in consciousness and so cannot be treated as mere negations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefinite (non-formulable) consciousness complements definite logical consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides definite consciousness expressible by logic, there is an indefinite consciousness which cannot be formulated; there are thoughts impossible to complete yet still real as normal affections of the intellect (providing an indefinite awareness of that which transcends distinct consciousness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: this indefinite consciousness allows a positive (though unformulable) awareness of the Non-relative/Absolute, thereby qualifying the strict logical claim that we can think only the relative. It preserves a residuary 'something' after abstraction of limits and conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognition is graded and depends on assimilation to prior categories
rubrics_metrics.description: An object is perfectly known only when it resembles previously observed things in all respects; in proportion to the respects in which it is unlike them is the extent to which it is unknown. Novel objects are known as far as they can be assimilated to existing classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: unknown animal might be classified at progressively coarser levels (mammal, vertebrate, living body, material object). Cognition develops from chaotic impressions to orderly classifications by frequent repetition and grouping; thus there can be no absolute 'first cognition' — cognition emerges gradually.
